Gastrointestinal diseases are health conditions that affect your gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Your GI tract is the path food takes through your digestive system — from your mouth to your rectum. It also includes your liver, pancreas and gallbladder. Some digestive system diseases cause problems that go away relatively fast with treatment. Others cause problems that are more serious. Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services. Policy GI diseases can be acute or chronic: * An acute GI disease is one that happens suddenly and lasts a short period of time. * A chronic GI disease can affect you for many months or years. They can also be either functional or structural: * A functional GI disease is when your healthcare provider can’t see any physical or structural issues when they examine your digestive tract. * A structural GI disease is when your healthcare provider can see evidence of an issue when they examine you. Functional gastrointestinal diseases You’ve likely experienced several functional GI problems in your lifetime. Constipation, gas and diarrhea are examples of functional GI diseases. These types of GI diseases irritate your GI tract and lead to uncomfortable symptoms. Some of the most common causes of functional GI problems are: * Eating a diet low in fiber or high in processed foods * Not getting enough exercise * Traveling or other changes in your typical routine * Stress and anxiety * Holding your poop or not going as soon as you need to go * Taking certain medicines * Hormonal changes (like pregnancy or during menstruation) * Food sensitivities or eating something that didn’t “agree” with you Treatment for functional GI diseases usually involves lifestyle changes like eating more fiber-rich foods, getting more physical activity or avoiding triggers. Sometimes, functional problems go away on their own within a few days. Structural gastrointestinal diseases Structural GI diseases are typically more complicated. They tend to cause symptoms that last longer and don’t get better with lifestyle changes alone. Structural problems cause issues your provider can see such as inflammation or blockages. Common examples of structural GI diseases include hemorrhoids, colon polyps and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Causes of structural GI diseases are more widespread. What are the most common gastrointestinal diseases? Healthcare providers who specialize in gastrointestinal diseases are called gastroenterologists. Some of the most common GI conditions they treat include: Constipation Constipation causes hard-to-pass or infrequent bowel movements. You may strain or push hard to get your poop out. You can treat your constipation at home by drinking more water and eating more fiber. Over-the-counter laxatives can also be helpful. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is where your intestinal muscles contract more or less often than normal. Abdominal pain, gas and bloating are common symptoms. Treating IBS can involve changing your eating habits or taking medication that your provider prescribes. Hemorrhoids Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in your anus or rectum. Straining when having a bowel movement is the most common cause, but you can get them other ways, too. Avoiding constipation activities that cause straining can help hemorrhoids. Your healthcare provider can also remove large, painful or persistent hemorrhoids. Diverticular disease Diverticulosis is when small pouches (diverticula) form in the wall of your large intestine. When they become infected, it’s called diverticulitis. This can lead to bleeding and bowel obstruction. Treatment could involve eating more fiber, taking antibiotics or having surgery. Colon polyps and colon cancer Colorectal cancer is one of the most common cancers in the U.S. Colonoscopy screenings help detect the disease, sometimes long before symptoms appear. Almost all colorectal cancers begin as colon polyps, benign (noncancerous) growths in the tissues lining your colon and rectum. Screening for colorectal cancer is important and early detection of the disease gives you the best chance at a cure. Colitis There are several types of colitis, which are conditions that cause inflammation of your bowel. Colitis can cause diarrhea, rectal bleeding, abdominal cramps and urgency (frequent and immediate need to poop). Ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease are two common types of colitis. Celiac disease Celiac disease causes problems in your GI tract when you eat gluten, a protein found in wheat and grains. It can cause symptoms like stomach pain, gas and bloating. It’s also considered an autoimmune condition because your immune system attacks gluten when it’s in your small intestine. The attack can damage your intestine enough that it stops working properly. Gastritis Gastritis is inflammation in your stomach lining. You may have symptoms like loss of appetite, stomach pain or nausea. Infection, chemicals and autoimmune diseases are common causes. Most cases of gastritis improve within a few days with over-the-counter medication. Gastroenteritis Gastroenteritis is when inflammation spreads from your stomach into your intestines. It causes pain, vomiting and diarrhea. It usually happens when you have a bacterial infection from food poisoning or a virus like the stomach flu. Most people will have gastroenteritis a few times during their lives for various reasons. Acid reflux/GERD Acid reflux and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) is when acid from your stomach flows back up into your esophagus and throat. It causes a burning feeling that can feel like a sore throat. Medications, changing your eating habits and surgery are options for treatment. fetched_contents.text: Early signs of stomach cancer | Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center Like many cancer types, stomach cancer develops slowly over several years. But the early changes that occur first and that may lead to cancer rarely cause symptoms, so they often go undetected. As a result, most cases are not diagnosed until the cancer has already spread beyond the stomach to nearby lymph nodes and tissues as well as distant body areas, making treatment challenging. "In the United States, and here at Roswell Park, a lot of patients have cancer that occurs at the junction of the stomach and esophagus, called the GE junction," says gastroenterologist Kevin Robillard, MD, of Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center. Cancer in the GE junction is often associated with a history of acid reflux, which can cause Barrett’s Esophagus, a precancerous condition. Those who have been on acid reflux medications for months or years should be monitored for this condition. It’s important that people with acid reflux or those with a family history of stomach cancer be alert to any new stomach symptoms and address them as soon as possible. Symptoms to alert your doctor Cancers can start in different sections of the stomach, and each can cause different symptoms and have different treatments. Every patient may present a little differently, but some of the common symptoms include unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing and sometimes blood in the stool. Unintentional weight loss should raise a red flag, especially if you have a family history of stomach cancer. Some minority populations, such as Asian/Pacific individuals, have a higher incidence of stomach cancer and should be extra cautious and see their doctor. The weight loss may come about as a result of other symptoms such as abdominal pain, fullness of the stomach, or loss of appetite and nausea. The abdominal pain, typically in the upper abdomen, is usually kind of a vague pain, and becomes more severe when the cancer is more advanced. Difficulty swallowing, called dysphagia, can be another common symptom. At first, it might not seem like a problem. But, it can progress from problems with swallowing solids to having trouble with softer or even pureed foods and liquids. A person might not notice blood in their stool because it is usually hidden or occult bleeding. Patients usually don’t notice it, but they can keep losing blood and can become anemic. Sometimes a patient may see overt bleeding. The stool color changes to a mostly black, tarry color, though that is uncommon. If the cancer metastasizes, symptoms may appear related to those areas, such as enlarged liver or lymph nodes. The cancer also tends to spread to the peritoneum, a membrane inside the abdomen. Symptoms of this include distention of the abdomen, pain and a slowing down or obstruction of the bowels. Any stomach pain that lasts for more than a few weeks, or keeps coming back, should be checked out. Finally, if you experience blood in the stool or vomit, don’t delay. See a doctor immediately. Get a second opinion It’s important to seek a second opinion before treatment begins to ensure your diagnosis is correct and your treatment options are appropriate. Learn More Seeking quality cancer care Although a fecal occult blood test is used to screen for colorectal cancer, it is not used for gastric cancer screening. But if blood is detected with a fecal occult blood test, it does not automatically mean colon cancer. Your physician will need to investigate further to determine the cause of the blood. An upper GI endoscopy is the next step in diagnosis, and then a CT scan is used to look for cancer spread, especially to the peritoneum. "In patients where this has occurred, there may be an option to treat with a specialized procedure called cytoreductive surgery and HIPEC," says Dr. Patel. Roswell Park is one of few providers able to offer this treatment approach known as hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC), which infuses high doses of heated chemotherapy directly to the abdomen. There are several reasons for patients to seek stomach cancer treatment at Roswell Park, explains Dr. Robillard. “We have screening expertise, especially when there is a family history, and you may benefit from our genetic screening. Second, when diagnosed very early, we have interventional endoscopists with special skills and training to remove it. Third, if you need surgery, you want a center that performs these surgeries frequently, and our surgeons have more experience than many other centers. Finally, Roswell Park is an academic research center. I always recommend patients being treated at a community hospital receive a second opinion here, because you may have an opportunity to participate in a trial which can allow you to access treatment options you can’t get elsewhere.”

fetched_contents.text: Abdominal Pain: ER or Urgent Care? Nothing can ruin your day like coming down with a stomach bug or an unexpected bout of food poisoning. Often these issues and other forms of abdominal pain can be treated at home, with a bland diet, rest, and fluids. But other times, you may want to see a health care provider to ensure it’s not a serious health condition. Ronak V. Shah, MD, medical director of Mass General Brigham Urgent Care, discusses common types of stomach complaints and describes when it may be best to seek urgent care or visit an emergency department. If you have new-onset abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation, Dr. Shah recommends calling your primary care provider (PCP). If you don’t have a PCP or no appointments are available, he recommends going to urgent care. “I would encourage anybody who is having abdominal pain that is brand new to them or severe to see a doctor in person,” he says. Depending on your symptoms, health care providers evaluate abdominal pain in the following ways: * Taking vital signs like your temperature, blood pressure, and pulse or heart rate * Doing a physical exam of your abdomen to determine the location and severity of your pain * Discussing your family and medical history, including recent weight loss or gain * Conducting stool studies to diagnose parasites or bacterial infection * Drawing blood samples to look at enzymes that show how your organs are functioning * Making referrals to specialists like gastroenterologists, or to the ER if needed * Prescribing antibiotics or medications for nausea, diarrhea, constipation and more “These in-person exams are thorough, and we’ll get a better picture of what’s affecting the patient,” says Dr. Shah. For example, appendicitis is usually marked by severe pain in the lower right side of the abdomen. “But often, appendicitis starts off as a vague pain that’s located more generally instead. In urgent care, we can help identify things like that at an earlier stage and educate patients about what to watch out for before it becomes a true emergency,” he explains. Common stomach conditions and their symptoms

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of common stomach-related issues, with many overlapping symptoms but distinct patterns for different causes. The most common stomach problems include gastritis, acid reflux/GERD, IBS, irritable bowel syndrome, and other functional and structural conditions such as diverticulitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease, and stomach cancer [N1-R2][N1-F1][N1-R5]. The classic symptoms are often summarized as upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, bloating, fullness, indigestion, gas, or pain after eating [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R3]. Some conditions are more clearly tied to specific patterns: for example, gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining and may present with loss of appetite, stomach pain, or nausea [N1-R3][N1-R4]. Acid reflux/GERD is characterized by burning or heartburn-like sensations, often with a sour taste and discomfort after eating or when lying down [N1-R1][N1-F1]. IBS is marked by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits [N1-R5][N1-F1]. In contrast, structural problems such as diverticulitis or colon polyps may produce more localized pain, bloating, vomiting, or changes in bowel movement patterns [N1-F1][N2-R3].

A key distinction in the evidence is between functional and structural causes. Functional GI diseases are those in which the provider cannot see a physical or structural issue during examination, while structural diseases involve visible inflammation, blockage, or other physical abnormalities [N1-F1]. The evidence also explicitly differentiates between functional and structural disease types, noting that functional problems may improve with lifestyle changes alone and often resolve within a few days, whereas structural problems tend to be more persistent and may require medical intervention [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source explicitly lists examples of functional GI diseases such as constipation, gas, diarrhea, and IBS, and structural diseases such as hemorrhoids, colon polyps, and inflammatory bowel disease [N1-F1]. This is important for a patient-oriented explanation because it helps separate temporary or lifestyle-related issues from more serious structural concerns.

The evidence also suggests which symptoms are more likely to indicate a specific condition. For example, blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or pain that lasts for weeks or recurs are red flags that the evidence links to more serious illness [N2-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The Roswell Park source specifically states that persistent cramps, low back pain, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and blood in stool are concerning signs that should prompt evaluation [N2-F2]. For gastritis, the evidence points to classic symptoms such as indigestion, abdominal pain, nausea, feeling full too soon during a meal, and sometimes vomiting [N1-R4]. For acid reflux/GERD, the evidence emphasizes burning or heartburn-like sensations that can feel like a sore throat [N1-F1]. For IBS, the evidence emphasizes abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits [N1-R5]. For structural problems such as diverticulitis, the evidence points to sudden and strong stomach pain, bloating, vomiting, and possible bowel obstruction [N2-R3]. For stomach cancer, the evidence emphasizes symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, blood in stool, and vague upper abdominal pain that becomes more severe with advanced disease [N2-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports a practical conclusion: many common stomach issues are functional and can be managed with lifestyle changes, while others are structural and may require more direct investigation [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The most useful way to interpret symptoms is to separate transient, functional complaints from symptoms that suggest a serious underlying condition such as bleeding, obstruction, perforation, or cancer [N2-R1][N2-F2].

When to worry and next steps

The evidence shows that serious illness is indicated by several red flags. The most important ones are symptoms that persist for weeks or recur, blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, severe pain, and signs of obstruction or bleeding [N2-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Roswell Park specifically says that any stomach pain lasting more than a few weeks or coming back should be checked out, and that blood in stool or vomit is a clear reason to see a doctor immediately [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that persistent cramps, low back pain, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and blood in stool are concerning signs [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence links acute complications of colon cancer to bleeding, obstruction, and perforation, with associated symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, vomiting, and possible bowel obstruction [N2-R1]. These are all strong indicators that a provider should be consulted promptly.

The evidence also provides a clear distinction between when to see a doctor and when to watch and wait. Most stomach pain is mild and related to digestion, but symptoms such as severe pain, high fever, or vomiting blood require urgent care [N3-R3]. The Mass General Brigham source says that in-person care is usually better for new-onset abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation, and recommends calling a primary care provider or going to urgent care if no appointments are available [N3-F3]. It also says that seeing a provider in person is better because doctors can check vital signs and perform a physical exam [N3-F3]. The source further distinguishes emergency situations from urgent care cases, noting that severe stomach pain that makes it difficult to function, sudden onset, high fever, blood in stool or vomit, or trauma-related pain are reasons to go to the emergency room [N3-F3]. The HCA Florida source similarly states that serious causes requiring emergency care include peptic ulcers or perforation, with burning or sudden severe pain as a warning sign [N3-R5].

For emergency signs, the evidence is clear: blood in stool or vomit, severe pain that does not ease within 30 minutes, sudden onset of pain, high fever, and inability to tolerate food or drink are all red flags for immediate care [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3]. The source also explicitly warns not to ignore these red flags and recommends dialing 911 if necessary [N3-F3]. In practical terms, the evidence supports a two-step approach: if the person has a mild, transient complaint such as occasional indigestion or mild bloating, they may safely watch and wait while keeping track of symptoms [N3-F3]. But if the symptoms are severe, persistent, or associated with blood, weight loss, or severe pain, they should seek prompt medical evaluation [N3-F3][N2-F2].

The evidence also provides a useful next-steps framework. The Mass General Brigham source recommends starting with a primary care provider if there is new-onset pain, diarrhea, or constipation, and otherwise going to urgent care if no appointments are available [N3-F3]. It also notes that virtual care may be appropriate for previously diagnosed conditions such as GERD or IBS [N3-F3]. For emergency cases, the source says to go to the emergency room instead of urgent care if the symptoms are severe enough that the person cannot function normally, if there is sudden onset, high fever, blood in stool or vomit, or trauma-related pain [N3-F3]. The overall message is that the threshold for worry is not high: when symptoms are severe, persistent, or concerning, prompt care is important [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Diagnostic evaluation and investigations

The evidence shows that the main tests used to investigate stomach problems include endoscopy, biopsies, imaging, blood tests, and stool studies [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R5]. The NIDDK source specifically states that doctors may take biopsies during endoscopy tests to help diagnose the cause of GI bleeding and can treat active bleeding or prevent complications [N5-R2]. Mayo Clinic notes that an endoscopy can help determine the cause of digestive signs and symptoms such as heartburn, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, and other upper GI issues [N5-R4]. The evidence also points to imaging tests such as CT scans, colorectal transit studies, defecography, and lower GI series [N5-R1]. NHS states that gastroscopy is a type of endoscopy used to look for problems in the stomach, including stomach cancer [N5-R5].

The evidence supports interpreting test results in context because the choice of test depends on the suspected condition. Endoscopy is particularly useful for evaluating the upper GI tract and can directly visualize the stomach lining, esophagus, and duodenum [N5-R4]. Biopsies during endoscopy are important for confirming conditions such as gastritis, ulcers, or cancer [N5-R2]. Imaging tests are used when there is suspicion of structural disease, obstruction, or cancer spread [N5-R1]. Blood tests may be used to assess enzymes or organ function, while stool studies can help diagnose parasites, bacterial infection, or occult bleeding [N3-F3][N5-R1]. The Roswell Park source adds that upper GI endoscopy is the next step after detecting blood, and CT scans are used to look for cancer spread, especially to the peritoneum [N2-F2].

The evidence also makes clear when investigations are needed versus when they are not. For mild, transient symptoms such as occasional indigestion, bloating, or mild gas, the evidence suggests that in-person care is usually the best first step, but major investigations are not immediately required unless symptoms are severe or concerning [N3-F3]. In contrast, investigations are needed when there are red flags such as blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, persistent pain, or symptoms of obstruction, perforation, or cancer [N2-F2][N2-R1][N3-R3]. The evidence also emphasizes that the interpretation of tests should not be taken in isolation; the context of symptoms, the patient’s history, and the physical exam are essential [N3-F3][N5-R2]. The Mass General Brigham source explicitly says that providers evaluate abdominal pain in person by taking vital signs, doing a physical exam, discussing medical history, and using in-person diagnostics such as stool studies and blood tests before deciding whether to refer to specialists or to the ER [N3-F3]. This means that investigations are usually reserved for when the provider suspects a serious condition or needs to confirm a diagnosis rather than being used for every complaint.

Overall, the evidence supports a staged approach: start with a provider assessment, use endoscopy or imaging when structural disease is suspected, use biopsies and blood tests to help diagnose specific causes, and reserve major investigations for patients with red flags such as bleeding, obstruction, perforation, or persistent serious symptoms [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

- **Acid reflux/GERD** is characterized by burning or heartburn-like sensations, often with a sour taste and discomfort after eating or when lying down [N1-F1].
- **IBS** is marked by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits [N1-R5][N1-F1].
- **Structural problems** such as **diverticulitis** may produce sudden and strong stomach pain, bloating, vomiting, and possible bowel obstruction [N2-R3].
- **Stomach cancer** is associated with unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, blood in stool, and vague upper abdominal pain that becomes more severe with advanced disease [N2-F2].

### Key distinction: functional vs. structural causes
The evidence also clearly differentiates between **functional** and **structural** causes [N1-F1]:
- **Functional GI diseases** are those in which the provider cannot see a physical or structural issue during examination. Examples include constipation, gas, diarrhea, and IBS [N1-F1].
- **Structural GI diseases** involve visible inflammation, blockage, or other physical abnormalities. Examples include hemorrhoids, colon polyps, and inflammatory bowel disease [N1-F1].

In practical terms, this means:
- **Functional issues** may improve with lifestyle changes alone and often resolve within a few days [N1-F1].
- **Structural issues** tend to be more persistent and may require medical investigation or treatment [N1-F1].

---

## 2) When to worry and what red flags to watch for

The evidence strongly emphasizes that some symptoms are red flags for serious illness [N2-F2][N2-R1]. The most important red flags include:

### Red flags that suggest serious illness
- **Persistent or recurring symptoms** that last for weeks
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Unexplained weight loss**
- **Fatigue or weakness**
- **Severe pain**
- **Signs of obstruction or perforation**
- **Symptoms of cancer**, such as difficulty swallowing or vague upper abdominal pain that worsens over time

Roswell Park specifically states that any **stomach pain that lasts more than a few weeks** or **keeps coming back** should be checked out, and that **blood in stool or vomit** is a clear reason to see a doctor immediately [N2-F2]. It also notes that persistent cramps, low back pain, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and blood in stool are concerning signs [N2-F2].

### When to see a doctor versus when to watch and wait
The evidence suggests that most stomach pain is mild and related to digestion, but symptoms such as **severe pain**, **high fever**, or **vomiting blood** require urgent care [N3-R3]. The Mass General Brigham source says that in-person care is usually better for **new-onset abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation**, and recommends calling a primary care provider or going to urgent care if no appointments are available [N3-F3].

For mild, transient symptoms such as occasional indigestion, bloating, or mild gas, the evidence suggests that **watching and waiting** may be safe while keeping track of symptoms [N3-F3]. But if symptoms are severe, persistent, or associated with blood, weight loss, or severe pain, prompt medical evaluation is important [N2-F2][N3-F3].

### Emergency signs that require immediate care
The evidence is clear about **emergency signs**:
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Severe pain that does not ease within 30 minutes**
- **Sudden onset of pain**
- **High fever**
- **Inability to tolerate food or drink**
- **Trauma-related pain**

The source also explicitly warns not to ignore these red flags and recommends dialing 911 if necessary [N3-F3]. The HCA Florida source similarly states that serious causes requiring emergency care include **peptic ulcers or perforation**, with **burning or sudden severe pain** as a warning sign [N3-R5].

---

## 3) Practical patient advice and management

The evidence provides a clear starting point for dietary and lifestyle changes, along with safe home remedies and what to avoid [N4-R2][N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### Dietary and lifestyle changes to try first
- **For gastritis**, the evidence recommends **low-fat, non-acidic foods**, fruits and vegetables, fish, lean meats, caffeine-free teas, and easily digestible carbohydrates [N4-R2][N4-F4].
- **For acid reflux/GERD**, the evidence points to avoiding **fatty, fried, and spicy foods**, and recommends eating smaller, more frequent meals and not lying down after eating [N4-R1][N4-F4].
- **For IBS**, the evidence suggests avoiding **gluten-containing foods** and other trigger foods, and notes that the **FODMAP diet** is a common approach for avoiding gas-producing foods [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **For general stomach discomfort**, the evidence emphasizes that **diet and lifestyle changes** are central to prevention and relief [N6-R1].

### Safe home remedies and what to avoid
- **Eat slowly**, prefer **home-cooked meals**, and **avoid lying down after eating** [N4-F4].
- For IBS and gas, the evidence supports **avoiding trigger foods** and following a **bland or low-FODMAP diet** [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- The evidence also warns against relying on little evidence for specific dietary recommendations and advises consulting a doctor or nutritionist for individualized advice [N4-F4].
- It also cautions against eating **irregularly**, eating **leftover foods**, and eating **trigger foods** such as spicy, sweet, or salty foods [N4-F4].

### Lifestyle changes
- The **NHS** source says digestive problems can be prevented, relieved, and even banished by **simple lifestyle changes**, including **managing stress** [N6-R1].
- The **UChicago** source explains that **stress, worrying, and anxiety** are common causes of stomach discomfort and other GI symptoms, and that it is usually **temporary and not serious** [N6-R4].
- The evidence also highlights that **reassurance** is an important part of communication, especially when patients are worried about non-specific conditions [N6-R5].

### How to track symptoms and report them to a provider
The evidence supports keeping track of symptom patterns, severity, duration, and any changes in **bowel habits**, **weight**, or **energy levels** [N3-F3][N6-R3]. The Mass General Brigham source explicitly says providers evaluate abdominal pain by taking **vital signs**, doing a **physical exam**, discussing **family and medical history**, and using in-person diagnostics such as **stool studies and blood tests** [N3-F3]. It also recommends calling a primary care provider for **new-onset pain, diarrhea, or constipation**, and that virtual care may be appropriate for previously diagnosed conditions such as **GERD or IBS** [N3-F3]. If needed, providers may refer to specialists or to the **ER** [N3-F3].

---

## 4) Diagnostic evaluation and investigations

The evidence shows that the main tests used to investigate stomach problems include **endoscopy**, **biopsies**, **imaging**, **blood tests**, and **stool studies** [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R5]. The NIDDK source specifically states that doctors may take **biopsies during endoscopy** to help diagnose the cause of GI bleeding and can treat active bleeding or prevent complications [N5-R2]. Mayo Clinic notes that an **endoscopy** can help determine the cause of digestive signs and symptoms such as heartburn, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, and other upper GI issues [N5-R4]. The evidence also points to imaging tests such as **CT scans**, **colorectal transit studies**, **defecography**, and **lower GI series** [N5-R1]. NHS states that **gastroscopy** is a type of endoscopy used to look for problems in the stomach, including stomach cancer [N5-R5].

### How to interpret test results in context
The evidence supports interpreting test results in context because the choice of test depends on the suspected condition [N5-R2][N5-R4]. Endoscopy is particularly useful for evaluating the upper GI tract and can directly visualize the stomach lining, esophagus, and duodenum [N5-R4]. Biopsies during endoscopy are important for confirming conditions such as gastritis, ulcers, or cancer [N5-R2]. Imaging tests are used when there is suspicion of structural disease, obstruction, or cancer spread [N5-R1]. Blood tests may be used to assess enzymes or organ function, while stool studies can help diagnose parasites, bacterial infection, or occult bleeding [N5-R1][N3-F3].

### When investigations are needed versus when they are not
The evidence also makes clear when investigations are needed versus when they are not. For mild, transient symptoms such as occasional indigestion, bloating, or mild gas, the evidence suggests that **in-person care is usually the best first step**, but major investigations are not immediately required unless symptoms are severe or concerning [N3-F3]. In contrast, investigations are needed when there are **red flags** such as blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, persistent pain, or symptoms of obstruction, perforation, or cancer [N2-F2][N2-R1][N3-R3].

---

## 5) Bottom line for patients

If you have **stomach issues**, here’s what to remember:
1. **Most common issues** include gastritis, acid reflux/GERD, IBS, indigestion, gas, bloating, and more serious structural problems [N1-F1].
2. **Watch for red flags** such as persistent or recurring symptoms, blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, severe pain, or signs of obstruction or perforation [N2-F2][N2-R1].
3. **When to act**:
   - Call your doctor or go to urgent care for severe pain, high fever, vomiting blood, or blood in stool [N3-R3].
   - Go to the **emergency room** if the pain is sudden, severe, or makes it hard to function [N3-F3].
4. **What to try first**:
   - Stress reduction
   - Eating smaller, more frequent meals
   - Avoiding trigger foods such as fatty, spicy, or acidic foods
   - Following a bland or low-FODMAP diet if IBS is suspected
   - Keeping track of symptom patterns and any changes [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4].
5. **When to investigate**:
   - Endoscopy, biopsies, imaging, blood tests, or stool studies are used when symptoms are severe, persistent, or concerning [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].
   - Tests are usually reserved for patients with red flags rather than for every mild complaint [N3-F3].

## Final reassurance

If you’re worried about your symptoms, the evidence supports a balanced approach: many stomach issues are temporary and can be managed with lifestyle changes, but some symptoms are clear signals that you need prompt care [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. The best next step is to **talk to your doctor or healthcare provider** and describe your symptoms clearly so they can decide whether to reassure you, monitor you, or investigate further [N3-F3][N6-R2]. You’re not alone in this — and early care often makes a big difference.

# Final patient-oriented answer: Stomach issues

## 1) What are the most common stomach issues and their classic symptoms?

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of common stomach-related problems, with many overlapping symptoms but distinct patterns for different causes [N1-F1]. Among the most common issues are **gastritis**, **acid reflux/GERD**, **IBS**, **indigestion**, **gas**, **bloating**, and other structural problems such as **diverticulitis**, **ulcerative colitis**, **Crohn’s disease**, and **stomach cancer** [N1-R2][N1-F1][N1-R5][N2-R3][N2-F2].

### Classic symptoms
The evidence lists several common symptoms:
- **Upper abdominal discomfort**
- **Nausea or vomiting**
- **Bloating or fullness**
- **Indigestion**
- **Gas or bloating**
- **Abdominal pain**
- **Loss of appetite**
- **Heartburn or burning sensations**
- **Changes in bowel habits**
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Weight loss**
- **Persistent pain or recurring pain**

These symptoms can vary depending on the condition. For example:
- **Gastritis** is inflammation of the stomach lining and may cause loss of appetite, stomach pain, nausea, and feeling full too soon during a meal [N1-R3][N1-R4].
- **Acid reflux/GERD** is characterized by burning or heartburn-like sensations, often with a sour taste and discomfort after eating or when lying down [N1-F1].
- **IBS** is marked by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits [N1-R5][N1-F1].
- **Structural problems** such as **diverticulitis** may produce sudden and strong stomach pain, bloating, vomiting, and possible bowel obstruction [N2-R3].
- **Stomach cancer** is associated with unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, blood in stool, and vague upper abdominal pain that becomes more severe with advanced disease [N2-F2].

### Key distinction: functional vs. structural causes
The evidence also clearly differentiates between **functional** and **structural** causes [N1-F1]:
- **Functional GI diseases** are those in which the provider cannot see a physical or structural issue during examination. Examples include constipation, gas, diarrhea, and IBS [N1-F1].
- **Structural GI diseases** involve visible inflammation, blockage, or other physical abnormalities. Examples include hemorrhoids, colon polyps, and inflammatory bowel disease [N1-F1].

In practical terms, this means:
- **Functional issues** may improve with lifestyle changes alone and often resolve within a few days [N1-F1].
- **Structural issues** tend to be more persistent and may require medical investigation or treatment [N1-F1].

---

- **Severe pain**
- **Signs of obstruction or perforation**
- **Symptoms of cancer**, such as difficulty swallowing or vague upper abdominal pain that worsens over time

- **Stomach cancer** is associated with unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, blood in stool, and vague upper abdominal pain that becomes more severe with advanced disease [N2-F2].

### Key distinction: functional vs. structural causes
The evidence also clearly differentiates between **functional** and **structural** causes [N1-F1]:
- **Functional GI diseases** are those in which the provider cannot see a physical or structural issue during examination. Examples include constipation, gas, diarrhea, and IBS [N1-F1].
- **Structural GI diseases** involve visible inflammation, blockage, or other physical abnormalities. Examples include hemorrhoids, colon polyps, and inflammatory bowel disease [N1-F1].

In practical terms, this means:
- **Functional issues** may improve with lifestyle changes alone and often resolve within a few days [N1-F1].
- **Structural issues** tend to be more persistent and may require medical investigation or treatment [N1-F1].

## 1) What are the most common stomach issues and their classic symptoms?

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of common stomach-related problems, with many overlapping symptoms but distinct patterns for different causes [N1-F1]. Among the most common issues are **gastritis**, **acid reflux/GERD**, **IBS**, **indigestion**, **gas**, **bloating**, and other structural problems such as **diverticulitis**, **ulcerative colitis**, **Crohn’s disease**, and **stomach cancer** [N1-R2][N1-F1][N1-R5][N2-R3][N2-F2].

### Classic symptoms
The evidence lists several common symptoms:
- **Upper abdominal discomfort**
- **Nausea or vomiting**
- **Bloating or fullness**
- **Indigestion**
- **Gas or bloating**
- **Abdominal pain**
- **Loss of appetite**
- **Heartburn or burning sensations**
- **Changes in bowel habits**
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Weight loss**
- **Persistent pain or recurring pain**

These symptoms can vary depending on the condition. For example:
- **Gastritis** is inflammation of the stomach lining and may cause loss of appetite, stomach pain, nausea, and feeling full too soon during a meal [N1-R3][N1-R4].
- **Acid reflux/GERD** is characterized by burning or heartburn-like sensations, often with a sour taste and discomfort after eating or when lying down [N1-F1].
- **IBS** is marked by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits [N1-R5][N1-F1].
- **Structural problems** such as **diverticulitis** may produce sudden and strong stomach pain, bloating, vomiting, and possible bowel obstruction [N2-R3].
- **Stomach cancer** is associated with unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, blood in stool, and vague upper abdominal pain that becomes more severe with advanced disease [N2-F2].

### Key distinction: functional vs. structural causes
The evidence also clearly differentiates between **functional** and **structural** causes [N1-F1]:
- **Functional GI diseases** are those in which the provider cannot see a physical or structural issue during examination. Examples include constipation, gas, diarrhea, and IBS [N1-F1].
- **Structural GI diseases** involve visible inflammation, blockage, or other physical abnormalities. Examples include hemorrhoids, colon polyps, and inflammatory bowel disease [N1-F1].

In practical terms, this means:
- **Functional issues** may improve with lifestyle changes alone and often resolve within a few days [N1-F1].
- **Structural issues** tend to be more persistent and may require medical investigation or treatment [N1-F1].

## 2) When to worry and what red flags to watch for

The evidence strongly emphasizes that some symptoms are red flags for serious illness [N2-F2][N2-R1]. The most important red flags include:

### Red flags that suggest serious illness
- **Persistent or recurring symptoms** that last for weeks
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Unexplained weight loss**
- **Fatigue or weakness**
- **Severe pain**
- **Signs of obstruction or perforation**
- **Symptoms of cancer**, such as difficulty swallowing or vague upper abdominal pain that worsens over time

Roswell Park specifically states that any **stomach pain that lasts more than a few weeks** or **keeps coming back** should be checked out, and that **blood in stool or vomit** is a clear reason to see a doctor immediately [N2-F2]. It also notes that persistent cramps, low back pain, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and blood in stool are concerning signs [N2-F2].

### When to see a doctor versus when to watch and wait
The evidence suggests that most stomach pain is mild and related to digestion, but symptoms such as **severe pain**, **high fever**, or **vomiting blood** require urgent care [N3-R3]. The Mass General Brigham source says that in-person care is usually better for **new-onset abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation**, and recommends calling a primary care provider or going to urgent care if no appointments are available [N3-F3].

For mild, transient symptoms such as occasional indigestion, bloating, or mild gas, the evidence suggests that **watching and waiting** may be safe while keeping track of symptoms [N3-F3]. But if symptoms are severe, persistent, or associated with blood, weight loss, or severe pain, prompt medical evaluation is important [N2-F2][N3-F3].

### Emergency signs that require immediate care
The evidence is clear about **emergency signs**:
- **Blood in stool or vomit**
- **Severe pain that does not ease within 30 minutes**
- **Sudden onset of pain**
- **High fever**
- **Inability to tolerate food or drink**
- **Trauma-related pain**

The source also explicitly warns not to ignore these red flags and recommends dialing 911 if necessary [N3-F3]. The HCA Florida source similarly states that serious causes requiring emergency care include **peptic ulcers or perforation**, with **burning or sudden severe pain** as a warning sign [N3-R5].

## 3) Practical patient advice and management

The evidence provides a clear starting point for dietary and lifestyle changes, along with safe home remedies and what to avoid [N4-R2][N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### Dietary and lifestyle changes to try first
- **For gastritis**, the evidence recommends **low-fat, non-acidic foods**, fruits and vegetables, fish, lean meats, caffeine-free teas, and easily digestible carbohydrates [N4-R2][N4-F4].
- **For acid reflux/GERD**, the evidence points to avoiding **fatty, fried, and spicy foods**, and recommends eating smaller, more frequent meals and not lying down after eating [N4-R1][N4-F4].
- **For IBS**, the evidence suggests avoiding **gluten-containing foods** and other trigger foods, and notes that the **FODMAP diet** is a common approach for avoiding gas-producing foods [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **For general stomach discomfort**, the evidence emphasizes that **diet and lifestyle changes** are central to prevention and relief [N6-R1].

### Safe home remedies and what to avoid
- **Eat slowly**, prefer **home-cooked meals**, and **avoid lying down after eating** [N4-F4].
- For IBS and gas, the evidence supports **avoiding trigger foods** and following a **bland or low-FODMAP diet** [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- The evidence also warns against relying on little evidence for specific dietary recommendations and advises consulting a doctor or nutritionist for individualized advice [N4-F4].
- It also cautions against eating **irregularly**, eating **leftover foods**, and eating **trigger foods** such as spicy, sweet, or salty foods [N4-F4].

### Lifestyle changes
- The **NHS** source says digestive problems can be prevented, relieved, and even banished by **simple lifestyle changes**, including **managing stress** [N6-R1].
- The **UChicago** source explains that **stress, worrying, and anxiety** are common causes of stomach discomfort and other GI symptoms, and that it is usually **temporary and not serious** [N6-R4].
- The evidence also highlights that **reassurance** is an important part of communication, especially when patients are worried about non-specific conditions [N6-R5].

### How to track symptoms and report them to a provider
The evidence supports keeping track of symptom patterns, severity, duration, and any changes in **bowel habits**, **weight**, or **energy levels** [N3-F3][N6-R3]. The Mass General Brigham source explicitly says providers evaluate abdominal pain by taking **vital signs**, doing a **physical exam**, discussing **family and medical history**, and using in-person diagnostics such as **stool studies and blood tests** [N3-F3]. It also recommends calling a primary care provider for **new-onset pain, diarrhea, or constipation**, and that virtual care may be appropriate for previously diagnosed conditions such as **GERD or IBS** [N3-F3]. If needed, providers may refer to specialists or to the **ER** [N3-F3].

## 4) Diagnostic evaluation and investigations

The evidence shows that the main tests used to investigate stomach problems include **endoscopy**, **biopsies**, **imaging**, **blood tests**, and **stool studies** [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R5]. The NIDDK source specifically states that doctors may take **biopsies during endoscopy** to help diagnose the cause of GI bleeding and can treat active bleeding or prevent complications [N5-R2]. Mayo Clinic notes that an **endoscopy** can help determine the cause of digestive signs and symptoms such as heartburn, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, and other upper GI issues [N5-R4]. The evidence also points to imaging tests such as **CT scans**, **colorectal transit studies**, **defecography**, and **lower GI series** [N5-R1]. NHS states that **gastroscopy** is a type of endoscopy used to look for problems in the stomach, including stomach cancer [N5-R5].

### How to interpret test results in context
The evidence supports interpreting test results in context because the choice of test depends on the suspected condition [N5-R2][N5-R4]. Endoscopy is particularly useful for evaluating the upper GI tract and can directly visualize the stomach lining, esophagus, and duodenum [N5-R4]. Biopsies during endoscopy are important for confirming conditions such as gastritis, ulcers, or cancer [N5-R2]. Imaging tests are used when there is suspicion of structural disease, obstruction, or cancer spread [N5-R1]. Blood tests may be used to assess enzymes or organ function, while stool studies can help diagnose parasites, bacterial infection, or occult bleeding [N5-R1][N3-F3].

### When investigations are needed versus when they are not
The evidence also makes clear when investigations are needed versus when they are not. For mild, transient symptoms such as occasional indigestion, bloating, or mild gas, the evidence suggests that **in-person care is usually the best first step**, but major investigations are not immediately required unless symptoms are severe or concerning [N3-F3]. In contrast, investigations are needed when there are **red flags** such as blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, persistent pain, or symptoms of obstruction, perforation, or cancer [N2-F2][N2-R1][N3-R3].

---

## 5) Bottom line for patients

If you have **stomach issues**, here’s what to remember:
1. **Most common issues** include gastritis, acid reflux/GERD, IBS, indigestion, gas, bloating, and more serious structural problems [N1-F1].
2. **Watch for red flags** such as persistent or recurring symptoms, blood in stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, severe pain, or signs of obstruction or perforation [N2-F2][N2-R1].
3. **When to act**:
   - Call your doctor or go to urgent care for severe pain, high fever, vomiting blood, or blood in stool [N3-R3].
   - Go to the **emergency room** if the pain is sudden, severe, or makes it hard to function [N3-F3].
4. **What to try first**:
   - Stress reduction
   - Eating smaller, more frequent meals
   - Avoiding trigger foods such as fatty, spicy, or acidic foods
   - Following a bland or low-FODMAP diet if IBS is suspected
   - Keeping track of symptom patterns and any changes [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4].
5. **When to investigate**:
   - Endoscopy, biopsies, imaging, blood tests, or stool studies are used when symptoms are severe, persistent, or concerning [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].
   - Tests are usually reserved for patients with red flags rather than for every mild complaint [N3-F3].

## Final reassurance

If you’re worried about your symptoms, the evidence supports a balanced approach: many stomach issues are temporary and can be managed with lifestyle changes, but some symptoms are clear signals that you need prompt care [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. The best next step is to **talk to your doctor or healthcare provider** and describe your symptoms clearly so they can decide whether to reassure you, monitor you, or investigate further [N3-F3][N6-R2]. You’re not alone in this — and early care often makes a big difference.
